q: A 68-year-old man is admitted with community-acquired pneumonia and treated with intravenous fluids and antibiotics. On day 3 his urine output falls to 15 mL/hour. Baseline creatinine was 82 µmol/L; it is now 240 µmol/L. He is clinically euvolaemic with a blood pressure of 118/74 mmHg. Urinalysis shows no blood or protein. Microscopy reveals muddy-brown granular casts. Urinary sodium is 55 mmol/L and fractional excretion of sodium is 3.2%. He received a single dose of gentamicin and one contrast-enhanced CT scan. Which single finding most strongly supports a diagnosis of established acute tubular necrosis rather than pre-renal acute kidney injury?
options: Blood pressure of 118/74 mmHg
Rise in creatinine from 82 to 240 µmol/L
Recent contrast administration
Fractional excretion of sodium of 3.2% with muddy-brown casts
Oliguria with urine output of 15 mL/hour
explain: Acute tubular necrosis (ATN) is distinguished from pre-renal AKI by loss of tubular sodium-reabsorbing capacity. 🧪 In pre-renal states the tubules are intact and avidly retain sodium, giving a FENa <1% and urine sodium <20 mmol/L. Once ischaemic/nephrotoxic injury establishes ATN, tubules can no longer reabsorb sodium, so FENa >2% and urine sodium >40 mmol/L. The muddy-brown granular casts are sloughed necrotic tubular epithelial cells and are the classic urinary hallmark of ATN. Gentamicin and iodinated contrast are both recognised nephrotoxins here. 🔬 Oliguria, the absolute creatinine rise and recent contrast are all consistent with AKI but do not discriminate pre-renal from intrinsic disease. A normal blood pressure argues mildly against severe hypoperfusion but is non-specific. The combination of high FENa and granular casts confirms intrinsic tubular injury, guiding supportive management (avoid further nephrotoxins, optimise perfusion) rather than aggressive fluid resuscitation, which would be appropriate only if pre-renal physiology were present.

Once ischaemic/nephrotoxic injury establishes ATN, tubules can no longer reabsorb sodium, so FENa >2% and urine sodium >40 mmol/L. A.html: A blood pressure of 118/74 mmHg is normal and argues mildly against profound hypoperfusion, but it is entirely non-specific. Pre-renal AKI can occur despite a normal recorded blood pressure (e.g. relative hypovolaemia, sepsis-related vasodilatation), so this value cannot reliably separate pre-renal physiology from established tubular necrosis.

Pre-renal AKI can occur despite a normal recorded blood pressure (e.g. relative hypovolaemia, sepsis-related vasodilatation), so this value cannot reliably separate pre-renal physiology from established tubular necrosis.

B.html: The rise from 82 to 240 µmol/L confirms AKI stage 3 by magnitude but says nothing about mechanism. Both pre-renal AKI and ATN can produce this degree of creatinine elevation; indeed untreated pre-renal AKI progresses into ATN, so the absolute value cannot discriminate reversible from established tubular injury.

Many patients receive contrast without developing nephropathy, so this is a risk factor, not a diagnostic discriminator.

q: A 24-year-old man presents with two days of cola-coloured urine, five days after a sore throat. Blood pressure is 158/96 mmHg and he has mild peri-orbital oedema. Creatinine is 138 µmol/L, urine shows dysmorphic red cells and red-cell casts, and proteinuria is 1.2 g/24h. Serum C3 is markedly reduced with a normal C4; anti-streptolysin O titre is elevated. Renal biopsy, if performed, would be expected to show subepithelial 'humps' on electron microscopy. Which single statement best describes the expected clinical course?
options: Full recovery of renal function is expected in the majority of children and most adults, with C3 normalising within 8 weeks
Progression to end-stage renal disease occurs in over half of patients
Persistent hypocomplementaemia beyond 12 weeks is typical and reassuring
Recurrent macroscopic haematuria with each subsequent infection is the hallmark
Nephrotic-range proteinuria with hypoalbuminaemia dominates the course
explain: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) is an immune-complex mediated nephritic illness following group A streptococcal pharyngitis or skin infection. 🦠 Complexes deposit in a subepithelial location ('humps') and activate the alternative complement pathway, hence the characteristic low C3 with normal C4. The lead-in asks about prognosis: the natural history is generally excellent, especially in children, with spontaneous resolution of haematuria, hypertension and renal impairment over days to weeks. ✅ A key examiner point is that C3 normalises within 6–8 weeks; persistent hypocomplementaemia beyond this window should prompt reconsideration (e.g. C3 glomerulopathy or lupus). Adults have a slightly less benign course but most still recover. Management is supportive: control blood pressure and treat any ongoing infection. Progression to ESRD is uncommon. Recurrent visible haematuria with each infection describes IgA nephropathy, in which haematuria is synpharyngitic (concurrent with infection) rather than delayed by 1–2 weeks, and complement is typically normal — an important discriminator in the exam.

The lead-in asks about prognosis: the natural history is generally excellent, especially in children, with spontaneous resolution of haematuria, hypertension and renal impairment over days to weeks. ✅ A key examiner point is that C3 normalises within 6–8 weeks; persistent hypocomplementaemia beyond this window should prompt reconsideration (e.g. C3 glomerulopathy or lupus). Adults have a slightly less benign course but most still recover. Management is supportive: control blood pressure and treat any ongoing infection. Progression to ESRD is uncommon. Recurrent visible haematuria with each infection describes IgA nephropathy, in which haematuria is synpharyngitic (concurrent with infection) rather than delayed by 1–2 weeks, and complement is typically normal — an important discriminator in the exam.

A.html: PSGN carries an excellent prognosis, particularly in children: haematuria, hypertension and azotaemia resolve over days to weeks, and depressed C3 normalises within 6–8 weeks. Most adults also recover fully. This benign, self-limiting course with supportive management is the expected natural history.

B.html: Progression to ESRD in over half of cases is far too pessimistic for PSGN. A small minority of adults develop chronic kidney disease, but the overwhelming majority recover renal function. This figure would be more typical of untreated rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis, not classic post-streptococcal disease.

This figure would be more typical of untreated rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis, not classic post-streptococcal disease.

C.html: Persistent hypocomplementaemia beyond 12 weeks is not typical of PSGN and is a red flag: it should prompt investigation for C3 glomerulopathy (dense deposit disease) or lupus nephritis. In genuine PSGN, C3 is expected to normalise by 6–8 weeks, so ongoing low C3 is concerning rather than reassuring.

In genuine PSGN, C3 is expected to normalise by 6-8 weeks, so ongoing low C3 is concerning rather than reassuring.

D.html: Recurrent visible haematuria coincident with mucosal infections characterises IgA nephropathy, where haematuria is synpharyngitic and complement is normal. In PSGN haematuria follows infection by 1–2 weeks and does not typically recur with every subsequent infection, making this course inconsistent with the immune-complex, low-C3 picture described.

E.html: PSGN is a nephritic syndrome dominated by haematuria, hypertension, oedema and modest proteinuria (usually sub-nephrotic, as here at 1.2 g/day). Heavy nephrotic-range proteinuria with hypoalbuminaemia points instead to a nephrotic process such as minimal change or membranous nephropathy, not the picture described.

q: A 72-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease attends the emergency department feeling generally unwell. He takes ramipril, spironolactone and recently started trimethoprim for a urinary tract infection. Potassium is 7.1 mmol/L, creatinine 210 µmol/L, and bicarbonate 18 mmol/L. The ECG shows tall tented T waves, a broad QRS and flattened P waves. Which single intervention should be administered first to protect the myocardium?
options: Intravenous insulin with 50 mL of 50% dextrose
Nebulised salbutamol 10 mg
Intravenous calcium gluconate 10% 30 mL
Oral calcium resonium 15 g
Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 8.4%
explain: Severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes is a medical emergency because of the risk of ventricular fibrillation and asystole. ⚡ The first priority is myocardial membrane stabilisation with intravenous calcium (gluconate or chloride). Calcium raises the threshold potential, restoring the gradient between resting and threshold potentials that hyperkalaemia has narrowed, thereby reducing arrhythmia risk. It works within minutes but does not lower serum potassium, so it must be followed by potassium-shifting therapy. 🫀 After calcium, insulin–dextrose drives potassium intracellularly via Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase (the mainstay shifting therapy), with nebulised salbutamol as an adjunct. Removal of potassium from the body then follows — dialysis if refractory, or cation exchangers. The precipitants here are classic: ACE inhibitor, potassium-sparing diuretic (spironolactone), CKD and trimethoprim (which blocks the epithelial sodium channel like amiloride). Sodium bicarbonate has a limited role and is not first-line for cardioprotection. UK Renal Association guidance sequences treatment as: protect the heart (calcium) → shift (insulin/dextrose ± salbutamol) → remove.

A.html: Insulin–dextrose is the mainstay shifting therapy, driving potassium intracellularly via Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase within 15–30 minutes. However, it does not provide immediate myocardial protection; with ECG changes present, calcium must be given first to stabilise the membrane, followed by insulin–dextrose.

However, it does not provide immediate myocardial protection; with ECG changes present, calcium must be given first to stabilise the membrane, followed by insulin-dextrose.

B.html: Nebulised salbutamol shifts potassium intracellularly via β2-mediated activation of Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and is a useful adjunct, but its effect is modest and it does not stabilise the myocardium. It cannot substitute for the immediate cardioprotection provided by intravenous calcium when ECG changes are present.

It does not lower potassium, so shifting and removal therapies must follow, but cardioprotection is the immediate priority.

D.html: Calcium resonium (a cation exchange resin) removes potassium from the gut over many hours and has no acute cardioprotective or shifting effect. It plays a role only in the later 'removal' phase and is useless for the immediate arrhythmia risk posed by the ECG changes described.

E.html: Sodium bicarbonate has only a weak, unreliable potassium-lowering effect and is not recommended for acute cardioprotection. It may have a limited role in severe metabolic acidosis, but it does not stabilise the myocardium and should never take precedence over intravenous calcium when ECG changes are present.

q: A 34-year-old woman is investigated for fatigue and muscle weakness. She has a history of Sjögren syndrome. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.29, bicarbonate 15 mmol/L, and the arterial pCO2 is appropriately reduced. Potassium is 2.9 mmol/L and chloride 114 mmol/L. The serum anion gap is normal. Despite the systemic acidosis, urine pH is persistently 6.5. Abdominal imaging reveals bilateral nephrocalcinosis. Which single mechanism best explains this acid–base disturbance?
options: Impaired proximal tubular bicarbonate reabsorption
Failure of distal tubular hydrogen ion secretion
Aldosterone deficiency or resistance
Accumulation of unmeasured organic acids
Gastrointestinal bicarbonate loss from chronic diarrhoea
explain: Type 1 (distal) renal tubular acidosis arises from a defect in hydrogen-ion secretion by the α-intercalated cells of the distal nephron (H⁺-ATPase or its regulators). 🧬 Because the distal tubule cannot secrete protons, the urine cannot be acidified below pH 5.5 despite systemic acidaemia — the hallmark being a persistently high urine pH (>5.5) with a normal-anion-gap (hyperchloraemic) metabolic acidosis. This is a classic association with Sjögren syndrome and other autoimmune diseases. 🦴 Hypokalaemia occurs because impaired H⁺ secretion increases distal potassium secretion, and the chronic acidosis mobilises bone buffers and raises urinary calcium/citrate handling abnormalities, promoting nephrocalcinosis and calcium phosphate stones. Proximal (type 2) RTA, by contrast, causes bicarbonate wasting with a urine that can acidify once the filtered bicarbonate load falls, and is associated with Fanconi syndrome rather than nephrocalcinosis. Type 4 RTA is hyperkalaemic and results from hypoaldosteronism. Treatment of type 1 RTA is with oral bicarbonate or citrate, which also corrects the hypokalaemia and reduces stone formation.

Proximal (type 2) RTA, by contrast, causes bicarbonate wasting with a urine that can acidify once the filtered bicarbonate load falls, and is associated with Fanconi syndrome rather than nephrocalcinosis. Type 4 RTA is hyperkalaemic and results from hypoaldosteronism. Treatment of type 1 RTA is with oral bicarbonate or citrate, which also corrects the hypokalaemia and reduces stone formation.

A.html: Impaired proximal bicarbonate reabsorption is type 2 (proximal) RTA. Here the urine can acidify below 5.5 once the reduced filtered bicarbonate load is exhausted, and the condition associates with Fanconi syndrome (glycosuria, aminoaciduria, phosphaturia). Nephrocalcinosis is uncommon, making this inconsistent with the persistently alkaline urine and stones described.

B.html: Failure of distal α-intercalated cell H⁺ secretion defines type 1 (distal) RTA: the urine cannot acidify below 5.5 despite systemic acidaemia. This produces hypokalaemic hyperchloraemic (normal-gap) acidosis with nephrocalcinosis, and is classically associated with Sjögren syndrome — exactly the picture presented.

C.html: Aldosterone deficiency or resistance causes type 4 RTA, which is characterised by hyperkalaemia and typically a mild acidosis with an acidic urine. The profound hypokalaemia (2.9 mmol/L) and persistently alkaline urine here are the opposite of the type 4 picture, excluding this mechanism.

D.html: Accumulation of unmeasured organic acids (e.g. lactate, ketones, toxins) produces a raised anion gap acidosis. The anion gap here is normal and chloride is elevated, indicating a hyperchloraemic process from renal bicarbonate/acid handling, not organic acid accumulation.

E.html: Chronic diarrhoea causes a normal-anion-gap acidosis from gut bicarbonate loss, but the kidney responds appropriately by acidifying the urine (pH usually <5.5) and there is no nephrocalcinosis. The persistently alkaline urine and nephrocalcinosis in a patient with Sjögren syndrome point firmly to a renal tubular defect instead.

q: A 47-year-old man with a 30-pack-year smoking history presents with haemoptysis and breathlessness, then develops oliguria over 48 hours. Creatinine is 480 µmol/L. Urinalysis shows blood +++ and protein ++, with red-cell casts. Chest radiograph shows bilateral alveolar shadowing. Anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody is strongly positive; ANCA is negative. Renal biopsy demonstrates crescents in over 70% of glomeruli with linear IgG deposition along the glomerular basement membrane on immunofluorescence. Which single management strategy is most appropriate?
options: Plasma exchange with corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide
High-dose corticosteroids alone
Rituximab monotherapy
Supportive care and haemodialysis without immunosuppression
Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor and blood pressure control
explain: Anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture disease) is caused by autoantibodies against the α3 chain of type IV collagen in the glomerular and alveolar basement membranes, producing a pulmonary–renal syndrome of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and lung haemorrhage. 🫁 The linear IgG on immunofluorescence and circulating anti-GBM antibody are diagnostic; the crescentic biopsy indicates RPGN. This is a nephrological emergency. The evidence-based regimen combines urgent plasma exchange (to remove circulating pathogenic antibody), corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide (to suppress further antibody production). 🩸 Plasma exchange is the distinguishing feature versus ANCA vasculitis management and is time-critical: the chance of renal recovery falls sharply once patients are dialysis-dependent or creatinine is very high, but plasma exchange is still indicated when there is pulmonary haemorrhage regardless of renal prognosis. Immunosuppression alone (steroids ± cyclophosphamide) without plasma exchange is inferior for antibody removal. Rituximab may be considered in selected/refractory cases but is not standard first-line. Withholding immunosuppression risks fatal pulmonary haemorrhage and irreversible renal failure.

Plasma exchange removes circulating pathogenic anti-GBM antibody while steroids and cyclophosphamide suppress ongoing production. This triple approach is time-critical and is the only option that both clears antibody and controls the immune response, protecting kidneys and lungs.

This triple approach is time-critical and is the only option that both clears antibody and controls the immune response, protecting kidneys and lungs.

B.html: Corticosteroids alone suppress inflammation but neither remove the circulating pathogenic antibody nor adequately halt its production. Without plasma exchange and cyclophosphamide, patients remain at high risk of fatal pulmonary haemorrhage and progressive renal failure, so steroid monotherapy is inadequate for this pulmonary–renal emergency.

Without plasma exchange and cyclophosphamide, patients remain at high risk of fatal pulmonary haemorrhage and progressive renal failure, so steroid monotherapy is inadequate for this pulmonary-renal emergency.

C.html: Rituximab depletes B cells and can be considered in refractory or cyclophosphamide-intolerant cases, but it is not standard first-line therapy for anti-GBM disease and, used alone, fails to remove existing circulating antibody rapidly. The established evidence supports plasma exchange with steroids and cyclophosphamide as initial treatment.

D.html: Withholding immunosuppression exposes the patient to potentially fatal pulmonary haemorrhage and guarantees irreversible renal loss. Even when renal recovery is unlikely (dialysis-dependent), plasma exchange and immunosuppression are still indicated to control life-threatening lung bleeding, so pure supportive care is inappropriate here.

q: A 40-year-old man is found to be hypertensive at a routine check. Blood pressure is 162/98 mmHg. Examination reveals bilateral palpable flank masses. Creatinine is 118 µmol/L. Ultrasound shows multiple bilateral renal cysts and several hepatic cysts. His father died of a subarachnoid haemorrhage aged 55. Genetic testing confirms a mutation in the gene encoding polycystin-1. He asks what treatment might slow progression of his kidney disease. Which single agent has the strongest evidence for slowing decline in this condition?
options: Ramipril titrated to a low-normal blood pressure only
Allopurinol
Tolvaptan
Spironolactone
High-dose atorvastatin
explain: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is most commonly caused by mutations in PKD1 (polycystin-1), producing progressive bilateral cyst growth, hypertension, hepatic cysts and an association with intracranial (berry) aneurysms — hence the family history of subarachnoid haemorrhage. 💧 Cyst growth is driven by cyclic AMP, which is stimulated by vasopressin (ADH) acting on V2 receptors in the collecting duct, promoting fluid secretion and epithelial proliferation. Tolvaptan, a selective V2-receptor antagonist, blocks this pathway and is the agent with the strongest evidence (TEMPO 3:4 and REPRISE trials) for slowing the rate of total kidney volume increase and eGFR decline. It is recommended by NICE for adults with CKD stage 2–3 and evidence of rapidly progressing disease. ⚠️ Its principal adverse effects are aquaresis (thirst, polyuria) and idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity, requiring liver monitoring. Blood pressure control (usually with ACE inhibitors, targeting tighter control in younger patients) is important supportive therapy but does not match tolvaptan for disease-specific benefit. Statins, allopurinol and spironolactone have no established role in slowing ADPKD progression.

The disease-specific evidence for reducing kidney volume growth and eGFR decline lies with tolvaptan, so ramipril alone is not the strongest answer.
A.text: Rigorous blood pressure control with an ACE inhibitor is important supportive management and modestly slows progression, but it does not target the cyst-growth pathway. The disease-specific evidence for reducing kidney volume growth and eGFR decline lies with tolvaptan, so ramipril alone is not the strongest answer.

B.html: Allopurinol lowers urate and is used in gout; although hyperuricaemia can occur in CKD, allopurinol has no established role in slowing ADPKD cyst growth or preserving renal function. It does not act on the vasopressin–cAMP pathway that drives this disease.

C.html: Tolvaptan, a V2-receptor antagonist, blocks vasopressin-driven cAMP generation that fuels cyst expansion. TEMPO 3:4 and REPRISE demonstrated slower total kidney volume growth and eGFR decline, and NICE recommends it for rapidly progressing ADPKD. It is the agent with the strongest disease-modifying evidence, requiring liver-function monitoring for idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity.

D.html: Spironolactone is an aldosterone antagonist used for resistant hypertension and heart failure. It has no proven effect on ADPKD cyst progression and, being potassium-sparing, carries hyperkalaemia risk in CKD. It does not address the vasopressin-driven mechanism of cyst growth.

E.html: Statins reduce cardiovascular risk and are appropriate for lipid management, but high-dose atorvastatin has not been shown to slow the progression of ADPKD in adults. It provides no disease-specific benefit for cyst growth compared with the trial-supported effect of tolvaptan.

q: A 58-year-old man presents with fatigue, bone pain and constipation. Investigations show haemoglobin 92 g/L, calcium 2.92 mmol/L, creatinine 320 µmol/L, and albumin 30 g/L. Serum protein electrophoresis reveals an IgG kappa paraprotein and serum free light chains are markedly elevated with an abnormal kappa:lambda ratio. Urine dipstick is negative for protein, yet a 24-hour urine collection shows 3.1 g of protein. Renal biopsy shows eosinophilic casts within distal tubules surrounded by multinucleated giant cells. Which single mechanism best explains his acute kidney injury?
options: Deposition of amyloid fibrils in the glomerular mesangium
Precipitation of filtered free light chains with Tamm–Horsfall protein forming tubular casts
Immune-complex deposition activating the classical complement pathway
Podocyte foot-process effacement causing selective albuminuria
Hypercalcaemia-induced afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction alone
explain: Cast nephropathy ('myeloma kidney') is the commonest cause of renal failure in multiple myeloma. 🧫 Overproduced monoclonal free light chains are filtered by the glomerulus and reach the distal tubule, where they co-precipitate with Tamm–Horsfall protein (uromodulin) to form obstructing, waxy eosinophilic casts that provoke a giant-cell reaction — exactly the biopsy description. A crucial exam clue is the discordant urinalysis: the dipstick detects albumin, not light chains, so it reads negative despite heavy light-chain proteinuria quantified on 24-hour collection or by free light-chain assay. 🔬 Contributing factors include dehydration, hypercalcaemia, loop diuretics and nephrotoxins, all of which promote cast formation. Management is urgent: aggressive rehydration, correction of hypercalcaemia, avoidance of nephrotoxins and prompt anti-myeloma therapy (e.g. bortezomib-based) to reduce light-chain production. AL amyloidosis and light-chain deposition disease are alternative renal manifestations but produce glomerular pathology with Congo-red positivity (amyloid) rather than distal tubular casts with giant cells. Isolated hypercalcaemia can impair GFR but does not produce the characteristic cast histology.

A.html: Renal AL amyloidosis deposits Congo-red-positive fibrils in the glomerular mesangium and vessel walls, producing nephrotic-range albuminuria. The biopsy here shows distal tubular casts with giant cells, not glomerular amyloid, so amyloid deposition does not explain this picture despite being another myeloma-related renal lesion.

C.html: Immune-complex deposition with classical complement activation underlies conditions such as post-infectious or lupus nephritis, producing a proliferative glomerulonephritis with low complement. It does not generate distal tubular protein casts with giant cells, and there is nothing in the myeloma picture to implicate immune-complex glomerular injury.

D.html: Podocyte foot-process effacement causes selective albuminuria (minimal change disease) and would give a strongly positive dipstick. Here the dipstick is negative because the proteinuria is light chains, not albumin, so a podocytopathy cannot account for the findings or the tubular cast histology.

E.html: Hypercalcaemia does impair GFR via afferent vasoconstriction and volume depletion and is a genuine contributor, but it acts as a precipitant rather than the primary lesion. It cannot by itself produce the pathognomonic eosinophilic casts with giant cells that define cast nephropathy, so it is not the best single mechanism.

q: An 82-year-old woman is admitted with confusion and reduced oral intake over a week. She takes bendroflumethiazide and sertraline. She is clinically euvolaemic. Sodium is 118 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, and creatinine 74 µmol/L. Serum osmolality is 248 mosmol/kg, urine osmolality 480 mosmol/kg, and urine sodium 52 mmol/L. Thyroid and short Synacthen tests are normal. Which single next step in management is most appropriate for her hyponatraemia?
options: Rapid correction with hypertonic 3% saline to normalise sodium within 12 hours
Intravenous 0.9% saline at 250 mL/hour
Commence tolvaptan immediately
Fluid restriction to 750–1000 mL per day and stop contributing drugs
Administer intravenous furosemide with potassium replacement
explain: Euvolaemic hyponatraemia with concentrated urine (osmolality >100 mosmol/kg) and urine sodium >30 mmol/L, after excluding hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency, is the classic biochemical picture of the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis (SIADH). 💧 Here it is likely drug-induced: both thiazides and SSRIs (sertraline) are recognised precipitants. The cornerstone of management for chronic, mildly symptomatic SIADH is fluid restriction (typically 750–1000 mL/day) together with removal of the offending drugs. ⚠️ Rapid correction is dangerous: over-swift rises in sodium risk osmotic demyelination syndrome, so the rate should not exceed roughly 8–10 mmol/L in 24 hours (lower in high-risk patients). Hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptoms such as seizures or coma, given cautiously in small aliquots. Isotonic saline is ineffective or can worsen SIADH because the kidney excretes the sodium while retaining water. Tolvaptan is a second-line option if fluid restriction fails, not first-line, and requires careful monitoring to avoid over-rapid correction. Loop diuretics are not first-line here.

Hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptoms such as seizures or coma, given cautiously in small aliquots. This patient is confused but not seizing or comatose, so aggressive overcorrection is both unnecessary and dangerous.

Volume expansion is inappropriate in a euvolaemic patient with this urine chemistry.

It is not the first step before simpler measures — fluid restriction and stopping the causative drugs — have been tried.

First-line management is fluid restriction to 750–1000 mL/day and withdrawing the offending drugs, allowing safe, gradual correction of sodium.

The initial, evidence-based step is fluid restriction with removal of the precipitating thiazide and SSRI.

q: A 6-year-old boy is brought to hospital with bloody diarrhoea that began five days ago, now settling, but he has become pale, lethargic and passed very little urine. Haemoglobin is 78 g/L, platelets 45 ×10⁹/L, and creatinine 190 µmol/L. Blood film shows fragmented red cells (schistocytes). Lactate dehydrogenase is elevated and the direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test is negative. Coagulation screen (PT and APTT) is normal. Which single organism is most commonly responsible for this presentation?
options: Escherichia coli O157:H7
Streptococcus pneumoniae
Salmonella typhi
Neisseria meningitidis
Clostridioides difficile
explain: Haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS) is defined by the triad of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury. 🦠 The Coombs-negative haemolysis with schistocytes and raised LDH indicates mechanical red-cell fragmentation in a thrombotic microangiopathy, while the normal PT/APTT distinguishes it from disseminated intravascular coagulation. In a child with a preceding bloody diarrhoeal illness, the cause is typically Shiga toxin–producing Escherichia coli, classically serotype O157:H7 (also Shigella dysenteriae). The Shiga toxin damages glomerular endothelial cells, triggering platelet-fibrin microthrombi, red-cell shearing and glomerular ischaemia. 💊 Management of typical (D+) HUS is largely supportive: careful fluid and electrolyte balance, and renal replacement therapy if needed. Antibiotics are generally avoided, as they may increase toxin release and worsen outcome, and antimotility agents should not be given. Most children recover renal function. Pneumococcal HUS and atypical (complement-mediated) HUS are important but far less common causes; the latter is treated with the complement inhibitor eculizumab.

In a child with a preceding bloody diarrhoeal illness, the cause is typically Shiga toxin–producing Escherichia coli, classically serotype O157:H7 (also Shigella dysenteriae). The Shiga toxin damages glomerular endothelial cells, triggering platelet-fibrin microthrombi, red-cell shearing and glomerular ischaemia. 💊 Management of typical (D+) HUS is largely supportive: careful fluid and electrolyte balance, and renal replacement therapy if needed. Antibiotics are generally avoided, as they may increase toxin release and worsen outcome, and antimotility agents should not be given. Most children recover renal function. Pneumococcal HUS and atypical (complement-mediated) HUS are important but far less common causes; the latter is treated with the complement inhibitor eculizumab.

Its toxin injures glomerular endothelium, producing the microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and AKI seen here after a bloody diarrhoeal prodrome. Management is supportive; antibiotics are generally avoided as they may worsen toxin release.

B.html: Streptococcus pneumoniae can cause a rare atypical HUS (via neuraminidase exposing the Thomsen–Friedenreich antigen), typically after invasive pneumonia or meningitis, and the direct Coombs test is often positive. It does not fit a bloody-diarrhoea prodrome with a negative Coombs test, so it is far less likely here.

The schistocytic haemolytic-uraemic picture after bloody diarrhoea points to Shiga-toxin E. coli, not typhoid.

The normal PT/APTT here excludes DIC, and there is no meningitic or septic picture, so meningococcus does not explain this HUS presentation.

The bloody diarrhoea followed by the haemolytic-uraemic triad in a young child is characteristic of E. coli O157, not C. difficile.

q: A 62-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension is started on ramipril for proteinuria. Two weeks later his creatinine has risen from 110 to 190 µmol/L. He has widespread vascular disease and an abdominal bruit. Renal ultrasound shows a 2 cm discrepancy in kidney size, with the smaller kidney measuring 8.5 cm. He is normokalaemic and clinically euvolaemic. Which single mechanism best explains the deterioration in renal function after starting the ACE inhibitor?
options: Acute interstitial nephritis triggered by the ACE inhibitor
Direct nephrotoxic tubular injury from ramipril
Loss of angiotensin II–mediated efferent arteriolar constriction reducing glomerular filtration pressure
ACE inhibitor–induced afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction
Rhabdomyolysis precipitated by the ACE inhibitor
explain: Bilateral renal artery stenosis (or stenosis in a single functioning kidney) should be suspected when an ACE inhibitor or ARB causes an abrupt, significant rise in creatinine, especially in a vasculopath with an abdominal bruit and asymmetric kidneys. 🩺 In a stenosed kidney, perfusion pressure is reduced, so glomerular filtration is maintained by angiotensin II–mediated constriction of the efferent arteriole, which preserves the transglomerular pressure gradient. When an ACE inhibitor blocks angiotensin II production, the efferent arteriole dilates, intraglomerular pressure falls, and GFR drops — hence the creatinine rise. ⚙️ A rise of up to ~25–30% may be tolerated, but a steep jump like this warrants investigation (e.g. MR or CT angiography) and usually withdrawal of the drug. Atherosclerotic renovascular disease is the commonest cause in older patients; fibromuscular dysplasia predominates in younger women. Revascularisation (angioplasty/stenting) has not shown clear benefit over medical therapy in most cases (ASTRAL, CORAL trials), so management is usually medical with careful drug selection. This is a functional, haemodynamic effect — not interstitial nephritis, direct tubular toxicity or rhabdomyolysis.

A.html: Acute interstitial nephritis is an immune-mediated reaction (classically with eosinophilia, rash, sterile pyuria and white-cell casts) developing over days to weeks. The clinical picture here — vasculopathy, abdominal bruit, asymmetric kidneys and an abrupt creatinine rise immediately on starting an ACE inhibitor — points to a haemodynamic renovascular mechanism, not interstitial inflammation.

B.html: ACE inhibitors are not directly tubulotoxic; they do not cause acute tubular necrosis by a nephrotoxic mechanism. The creatinine rise reflects a reversible fall in glomerular filtration pressure from efferent arteriolar dilatation in a stenosed kidney, not structural tubular injury.

C.html: In renal artery stenosis, reduced perfusion pressure makes GFR dependent on angiotensin II–mediated efferent arteriolar constriction. An ACE inhibitor removes this constriction, the efferent arteriole dilates, intraglomerular pressure falls and GFR drops — producing the abrupt creatinine rise seen in this vasculopath with asymmetric kidneys and a bruit.

An ACE inhibitor removes this constriction, the efferent arteriole dilates, intraglomerular pressure falls and GFR drops - producing the abrupt creatinine rise seen in this vasculopath with asymmetric kidneys and a bruit.

D.html: ACE inhibitors act on the efferent, not the afferent, arteriole. The afferent tone is governed largely by prostaglandins and myogenic autoregulation; it is NSAIDs that constrict the afferent arteriole. Attributing the effect to afferent vasoconstriction misplaces the mechanism responsible for the fall in filtration pressure.

E.html: Rhabdomyolysis causes AKI through myoglobin-induced tubular injury and would present with muscle symptoms, grossly elevated creatine kinase and pigmenturia. ACE inhibitors do not precipitate rhabdomyolysis, and none of these features are present, so this mechanism does not fit the renovascular scenario described.
